lessons.title: ICT and Emerging Technologies
lessons.notes_html:
ICT stands for Information and Communication Technology. It refers to all the tools and systems we use to share information and communicate with each other.

What ICT Includes

  • Computers — desktops, laptops and servers used for processing and storing data.
  • Internet — a global network that allows communication, information sharing and access to online services.
  • Mobile devices — smartphones and tablets that enable communication and access to information on the go.
  • Software — applications and programs that perform specific tasks, such as word processing, data analysis and communication.
  • Networking equipment — routers, switches and modems that connect devices and allow data to be transmitted across networks.
  • Cloud computing — online services that store and manage data and applications over the internet, rather than on local devices.

Emerging Technologies

Emerging technologies are new and exciting tools or ideas that are just starting to be used and could change the way we do things in the future. They are still being developed, but they have the potential to make a big impact on our lives. Their characteristics are: innovation (new ideas that push the boundaries of what is possible), potential for impact on industries and society, early adoption (not yet widespread), rapid evolution (they change quickly as research progresses) and an interdisciplinary nature (they combine knowledge from different fields).

Key Points

  • ICT means Information and Communication Technology.
  • Emerging technologies are new, fast-changing and not yet widespread.
  • Robotics, AI, 3D printing, VR, 5G and cloud computing are emerging technologies.

lessons.title: AI, Machine Learning and Robotics
lessons.notes_html:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a branch of computer science that uses algorithms, computational power and data to generate machines that can achieve tasks like human intelligence, such as visual sensitivity, speech recognition, translating written and spoken language, decision making, learning, problem solving, planning, reasoning and classifying patterns. John McCarthy is known as the Father of AI.

Machine Learning

Machine Learning (ML) is a branch of artificial intelligence that uses algorithms to learn from data and improve the performance of AI, such as predicting outcomes and the future. For example, a model that learns from the inputs 2, 3 and 4 giving outputs 4, 9 and 16 can predict that the output of 5 will be 25, because the outputs are the squares of the inputs.

AIML
The wider branch of computer science that makes machines able to perform tasks like human intelligence.A branch of AI: the part that uses algorithms to learn from data and improve performance, for example by predicting outcomes.

Robotics and Self-Driving Cars

Robotics is a field of technology that involves the design, construction, operation and use of robots. Robots are machines that can be programmed to perform tasks autonomously or semi-autonomously. Self-driving cars operate without the need for a human driver; they use a combination of sensors, cameras, radar and AI to understand their surroundings, make decisions and drive safely.

Key Points

  • AI makes machines perform tasks like human intelligence.
  • ML is a branch of AI that learns from data.
  • Robots are programmable machines that work autonomously or semi-autonomously.

3D printing, also known as additive manufacturing, is a method of creating a three-dimensional object layer-by-layer using a computer-created design. Instead of ink, 3D printers use materials like plastic, metal or resin to create solid objects. The first 3D printer was invented in 1983.

Holograms, 5G and Cloud

  • Holographic imaging — a three-dimensional projection which can be seen without using cameras or glasses; holography typically uses laser light to record and reconstruct images, and medical students are now being taught using this technology.

  • Cloud computing — a technology that allows users to access and manage computing resources over the internet rather than using local servers or personal computers. Its key features are on-demand access, scalability, cost-efficiency, accessibility from any device with an internet connection, and automatic updates.

Key Points

  • 3D printing builds objects layer by layer from plastic, metal or resin.
  • VR creates a full digital world; AR adds digital elements to the real world.

lessons.title: Evolution of ICT and the Processor
lessons.notes_html:
The evolution of ICT is a story of rapid advancements that transformed how we access, process and communicate information.

Stages of Evolution

  • Early computing (1940s-1950s) — mainframe computers: large, expensive computers used mainly by governments and large organizations. First generation computers used vacuum tubes for circuitry and magnetic drums for memory.
  • Personal computers (1960s-1970s) — PCs, also called micro computers, designed for a single consumer, used for word processing, multimedia playback, internet browsing and gaming.
  • Internet and Web era (1980s-1990s) — networking technologies connected computers over long distances through LANs and WANs, and the World Wide Web, introduced in the early 1990s, made the internet accessible to the general public.
  • Mobile and wireless technology (2000s) — smartphones combined computing power with mobile phones; Wi-Fi and 4G LTE made it easier to connect on the go.
  • Emerging technologies (2020s and beyond) — AI and ML, 5G networks, and the Internet of Things (IoT), which connects everyday objects to the internet.

The Processor

The processor is often called the brain of the computer. Its basic job is to receive input, process it and provide the appropriate output, because it executes instructions that run programs and perform calculations. Each new processor generation brings improvements in speed, efficiency and computing capability: early processors such as the Intel 4004 and Intel 8086 were large and simple; later generations added multi-core processors, better cache memory, integrated graphics and support for new technologies like DDR5 memory.

Key Points

  • ICT grew from mainframes to PCs, the Web, smartphones and now AI and IoT.
  • The processor is the brain of the computer.
  • Every processor generation is faster and more capable than the one before.

lessons.title: Computer Ports: Serial, Parallel, USB, HDMI and PCIe
lessons.notes_html:
A computer port is a jack or socket used for communication between the computer and its peripheral (input/output) devices, like a mouse, keyboard, monitor, printer, speaker or flash drive.

Serial PortParallel Port
An interface through which transmission of data is one bit at a time over a single communication line.An interface through which data is transferred in or out using more than one communication line or wire. The printer port is an example of a parallel port.

USB

USB stands for Universal Serial Bus. A USB port can be used to transfer data, connect peripherals and even act as a power supply for devices connected to it. There are four kinds of USB ports: Type A (rectangular, 4-pin, found on computers, gaming consoles and TVs), Type B or mini-USB, Type C and Micro USB. USB 3.0 is the common standard and supports a data rate of 400 MBps; USB 3.1 supports up to 10 Gbps. Type C is the latest USB, with 24 pins, and is supposed to replace Types A and B.

HDMI, e-SATA and PCIe

  • HDMI (High-Definition Media Interface) transmits audio and video on a single cable to monitors, HDTVs, Blu-Ray players, gaming consoles and projectors. It has a 19-pin connector. The book's update notes HDMI 2.1, with 48 Gbps bandwidth, supporting 4K and 8K at 120 Hz.
  • e-SATA (external Serial Advanced Technology Attachment) connects external storage devices like hard drives and SSDs.
  • PCI Express (PCIe) is short for Peripheral Component Interconnect Express: a high-speed interface standard for connecting graphics cards, SSDs, network cards and other expansion cards to the motherboard.

Key Points

  • A port is a jack or socket that connects peripherals to the computer.
  • Serial sends one bit at a time; parallel uses more than one wire.
  • USB Type C is the latest USB; HDMI carries audio and video on one cable.

lessons.title: Memory, Expansion Slots, Networks and Peripherals
lessons.notes_html:
Computer memory refers to the physical components within a computer that store data and instructions, either temporarily or permanently.

RAMROM
Random Access Memory. A type of volatile memory: it only stores data while the computer is powered on, temporarily holds the data and instructions the CPU needs to access quickly, and all data in RAM is lost once the computer is turned off.Read-Only Memory. A type of non-volatile memory: it retains its data even when the computer is powered off, and stores crucial data and instructions required for the computer to boot up, like the BIOS (Basic Input/Output System). Data in ROM cannot be easily modified or erased.

So volatile memory loses its contents when the power goes off, while non-volatile memory retains its data. RAM has two types: SRAM, made of transistors, faster and more expensive, which does not need refreshing; and DRAM, made of capacitors, slower and cheaper, which needs refreshing to save information.

Expansion Slots

Expansion slots, or bus slots, are slots inside a computer on the motherboard that allow additional components to be connected through an expansion card. The most used slots are: AGP (Accelerated Graphics Port) for the graphics card; AMR for modem and sound card; ISA (Industry Standard Architecture), used in early personal computers for network, sound and video cards; and PCI (Peripheral Component Interconnect), used for network card, SCSI, sound card and video card.

Networks

A network is a system that contains two or more computers connected together through cables, telephone lines, radio waves, satellites or infrared light beams. Connected devices are called nodes. A LAN (Local Area Network) is a private network connecting devices close together, like at home, office or in a building; a WAN (Wide Area Network) is a virtual network over the public internet. Advantages of a network are file sharing, hardware sharing (printers, scanners, CD-ROMs, modems, hard disks) and application sharing. Its disadvantages include loss of data from network faults, work depending on the network, risk of hacking, risk of virus and network cost.

Peripherals

A computer peripheral is any device that connects to the computing unit but is not part of the computing unit. The computing unit consists of the CPU, the motherboard and the power supply. Peripherals are detachable and can be replaced. There are three types: input devices (keyboard, mouse, microphone, webcam, joystick, light pen, scanner), output devices (monitor, printer, speakers, headphones, projector) and input/output and storage devices (external hard drive, USB flash drive, memory card, optical drive).

Key Points

  • RAM is volatile and temporary; ROM is non-volatile and holds the BIOS.
  • Two or more connected computers form a network; its devices are nodes.
  • Peripherals are detachable devices outside the computing unit.

lessons.title: The Word Window: Title Bar, Ribbon and Rulers
lessons.notes_html:
To use MS Word well, you must know the parts of its window.

  • Title bar — a horizontal bar located at the top of a window. It displays the title of the software and the name of the current document.
  • Quick Access Toolbar — located at the top left of the MS Word window; it gives quick access to frequently used features, such as Save and Undo.
  • Ribbon — the toolbar at the top of the window that contains various commands and tools, organized into tabs (such as File, Home and Insert), each with its own set of tools. It is located below the Quick Access Toolbar and the Title Bar.
  • Rulers — used to measure the dimensions of the document. The horizontal ruler is displayed at the top of the page and the vertical ruler at the left-hand side.
  • Insertion point (cursor) — the flashing cursor where typed text appears.
  • Status bar — the bar at the bottom of the window showing document information such as page number and word count, with the view buttons and the zoom slider at its right end.

Opening and Saving

To open a file, press Ctrl + O. To create a new document, press Ctrl + N. To select a word, double-click it; to select a sentence, press Ctrl and click in the sentence.

Key Points

  • The Title bar is at the top; the Quick Access Toolbar is at the top left.
  • The Ribbon holds commands organized into tabs.
  • Ctrl + O opens a file; Ctrl + N creates a new document.

lessons.notes_html:
A font is a graphical representation of text, of different typeface, font size or color. Font size is a number that indicates how many points are in the height of the text.

Bold, Italic and Underline

BoldItalic
Makes the selected text thick and dark so it stands out. Shortcut: Ctrl + B.Slants the selected text to the side. Shortcut: Ctrl + I.

Underline (Ctrl + U) draws a line under the selected text. To apply any of these: select the text, then click the Bold, Italic or Underline button in the Home tab, or use the shortcut key.

Change Case

  • Sentence case — text starts with a capital letter, like a sentence.
  • lowercase — text is all lowercase, with no capital letters.
  • UPPERCASE — text is all uppercase, with all capital letters.
  • Capitalize Each Word — the first letter of each word is capitalized.
  • Toggle Case — reverses the case of whatever is selected.

Line and Paragraph Spacing

Line spacing is the distance between lines of text; wide line spacing can make text much more readable. A line spacing of 1 is as large as one line, and 2 is the size of two lines. To change it: select the lines, select the Home tab, select the line spacing button in the Paragraph section, and choose your desired line space from 1.0 to 3.0. Paragraph spacing can be changed with Add Space Before Paragraph or Remove Space After Paragraph in the same menu.

Key Points

  • A font is a graphical representation of text.
  • Font size is measured in points.
  • Ctrl + B bolds, Ctrl + I italicizes, Ctrl + U underlines.

lessons.title: Paragraphs, Tables, Headers and Printing
lessons.notes_html:
Alignment means how text flows in the page.

AlignmentMeaningShortcut
Left-alignedText aligned with the left edgeCtrl + L
CenteredText centered between the two edgesCtrl + E
Right-alignedText aligned with the right edgeCtrl + R
JustifiedText aligned with both the left and right edges; justification controls the spacing between wordsCtrl + J

Bullets, Numbering and Indentation

There are two kinds of lists: bulleted and numbered lists; their buttons are in the Paragraph group. Indenting paragraphs allows you to set text within a paragraph at different margins: First Line controls the left boundary for the first line of a paragraph; Hanging controls the left boundary of every line except the first; One Left (left indent) controls the left boundary for every line; and Right controls the right boundary for every line. Click the Indent buttons repeatedly to increase the indent, or use the Paragraph dialog box.

Tables, Shapes and Page Setup

A table in MS Word is a grid made up of rows and columns that helps organize and present information in a structured way; each box in the grid is called a cell. Create one from the Insert tab by selecting Table and choosing the rows and columns; move between cells with the Tab key. To write in a shape: Insert tab, Shapes icon, draw the shape, right-click inside it and select Add text. Page margins and orientation are set from the Layout (Page Layout) tab, in the Page Setup group: by default the orientation is Portrait and the page size is A4.

Header, Footer and Printing

Header and Footer both contain information such as page numbers, title and date. The Header is the area at the top of the page and the Footer is the area at the bottom; both repeat on the pages of the document. Add them from the Insert tab. Save saves a file by giving a file name and location for the first time, while Save As creates a copy of a document while keeping the original. To print: open the document, click File then Print (or press Ctrl + P), choose your options (copies, custom range, one sided or both sides, collated, orientation, page size, margins, pages per sheet), then click Print.

  • Alignment can be left, center, right or justified.
  • A table is a grid of rows and columns; each box is a cell.
  • Header is at the top of the page; Footer is at the bottom.

Multimedia presentations are often made using software like Microsoft PowerPoint and Google Slides.

Components of Multimedia

lessons.title: PowerPoint and Creating a Presentation
lessons.notes_html:
PowerPoint is a complete presentation program/application developed by Microsoft. PowerPoint offers word processing, drawing, graphing and presentation management tools. To start it: press the Windows Start button or the Windows key, type PowerPoint, and click PowerPoint or select it with the arrow keys and press Enter.

The PowerPoint Window

  • Title Bar — shows the presentation name.
  • Quick Access Toolbar — the small toolbar at the top left.
  • File tab (Backstage view) — the first tab at the left of the Ribbon.
  • The Ribbon — the band of tabs and command groups.
  • Slides Pane — the pane at the left showing slide thumbnails.
  • Placeholders — the boxes on a slide such as Click to add title and Click to add subtitle.
  • Notes pane — the area below the slide where speaker notes are written.
  • Status Bar — the bar where you can see the current position of the slide.

Slides and Layouts

A slide is a single page of a presentation; a presentation is made up of multiple slides, and by default a new presentation begins with one slide. To create a blank presentation: click the File tab, click New or press Ctrl + N, and click Blank Presentation. To add a slide: on the Home tab, in the Slides group, click the top half of the New Slide button to insert a slide with the same or the Title and Content layout, or click the bottom half to choose a layout such as Two Content. Anything on the slide is called an object, for example text, images, audio and video; collect all required objects on your computer before you start.

Key Points

  • PowerPoint is a presentation program developed by Microsoft.
  • A presentation is made of slides; a new one begins with one slide.
  • Scanning a virus is NOT a feature of MS PowerPoint.

lessons.title: Animation and Transition
lessons.notes_html:
Animations are visual effects which make your texts, images, shapes or charts come alive. Animation is the visual effect that adds movement and sound effects on a PowerPoint slide, such as on text, image, shape or tables. Animations are added from the Animation tab.

The Four Types of Animation

TypeMeaning
EntranceControls how an object appears on the slide. For example, text might fade in, or an image might slide in from the side.
EmphasisEffects that occur by a mouse click, such as spinning an object.
ExitControls how an object leaves the slide. For example, text might fade out, or an image might fly off the slide.
Motion PathsThe object moves within the slide along a predetermined path, like a circle.

Transition

Transitions are the animation-like effects used in PowerPoint presentations to remove one slide from the screen and display the next slide. So a transition is the effect that occurs when you move from one slide to the next slide, while an animation acts on objects within a single slide.

Key Points

  • Animations make objects on a slide come alive.
  • The four types are Entrance, Emphasis, Exit and Motion Paths.
  • A transition happens between slides; an animation happens on a slide.

lessons.title: Email and the Email Address
lessons.notes_html:
Email stands for Electronic mail. Email (electronic mail) is a way to send and receive messages and files (text, pictures and sounds etc.) across the Internet. It is the fastest communication source, and sending messages directly from one computer to another is called email. Ray Tomlinson, the Father of E-mail, implemented the first email program in 1971. To send and receive email, you must have an e-mail account, be connected to the internet, and have the e-mail address of those to whom you want to send email.

The Email Address

Each user of email is assigned a unique name, called an e-mail address. Email addresses are always written in a standard format that includes a username, the @ (at) symbol, and the email provider's domain, for example uniquename@domain.com.

PartMeaning

Computational Thinking (CT) is a way of solving problems using methods that are similar to how a computer processes information. It involves four main steps, which help you think logically and systematically, not just for programming but for solving all kinds of problems in everyday life.

lessons.title: Decomposition, Pattern Recognition and Abstraction
lessons.notes_html:
Decomposition is breaking down a big problem into smaller problems. For example, to clean the classroom, you divide the main task into sub-tasks: cleaning the tables first, then cleaning the chairs, arranging the classroom items, and so on. Even a scary-looking problem becomes easier when decomposed: the roots formula for a quadratic equation can be broken into small steps — work out b squared, then 4 times a times c, then b squared minus 4ac, then its square root, then -b plus or minus that root, and finally divide by 2a.

Pattern Recognition

Pattern Recognition is about finding similarities or repeating elements in different situations. For example, while learning multiplication, you might notice that multiplying by 2 always gives you an even number. That is a pattern, and spotting it helps you solve new problems in the future.

Abstraction

Abstraction means focusing on the most important details and ignoring the unnecessary ones. It is like drawing a map of your neighborhood where you only include the streets and important buildings, not every single tree or house. In problem solving, abstraction means extracting the relevant information required to solve the problem.

Key Points

  • Decomposition breaks a big problem into smaller, manageable parts.
  • Pattern recognition finds similarities and repeating elements.
  • Abstraction keeps only the important details.

lessons.title: Understanding and Planning a Problem
lessons.notes_html:
A problem definition is a question or statement that addresses a specific requirement. When a problem is written or defined clearly, with no hidden information, it is known as problem definition — and a clear understanding of a problem is already halfway to finding the solution.

The 5Ws

To understand a complex problem, we often use the 5Ws: What — what is the requirement or goal of the problem; Who — who will solve the problem; Why — the reason to solve the problem; When — the time required to solve the problem; Where — where we will use the solution of the problem.

Planning Strategies

  • Divide and Conquer — divide the problem into small parts.
  • Guess, Check and Improve — guess different solutions of the problem and improve them.
  • Act It Out — also called to-do tasks: make a list of all tasks to solve the problem.
  • Prototype (Draw) — draw a sample or diagram of the solution; it is not the final shape of the solution.
  • Candid Solution — a direct, unplanned solution used when we do not have enough time; it is not the actual solution, but it may be near to the real solution.

To find the best solution, check the desired output of the problem, the minimum number of steps, the minimum time used, and the minimum cost for the solution. More than one algorithm can solve a given problem.

Subroutines, Procedures and Functions

TermMeaning
SubroutineA self-contained section of program code that performs a specific task, as part of the main program.
ProcedureA subroutine that performs a specific task without returning a value to the part of the program from which it was called.
FunctionA subroutine that performs a specific task and returns a value to the part of the program from which it was called.

Key Points

  • Understand the problem first, using the 5Ws.
  • A procedure returns no value; a function returns a value.
  • The best solution is checked by output, steps, time and cost.

lessons.title: Algorithms: Characteristics and How to Write Them
lessons.notes_html:
An algorithm is a sequence of steps to solve a particular problem — a set of instructions in simple language. The word algorithm relates to the name of the Muslim mathematician Muhammad Ibne Musa Al-Khwarizmi, and it means a procedure or a technique. Software Engineers commonly use an algorithm for planning and solving problems, and the algorithm is the first approach to solve a problem.

Characteristics of an Algorithm

  • Input — an algorithm may or may not require an input.
  • Output — each algorithm is expected to produce at least one result.
  • Definiteness — each instruction must be clear.
  • Finiteness — the algorithm should terminate after a finite number of steps.

Advantages and Disadvantages

Advantages: an algorithm tells you exactly what to do; if you follow the steps correctly, you get the same result every time; it saves time by being organized and logical; and it makes big problems easier by breaking them into smaller pieces. Disadvantages: algorithms are not flexible and only work for specific situations; a good algorithm takes time and effort to create; an algorithm cannot handle surprises; and mistakes in creating or following it can give the wrong result.

How to Write an Algorithm

  • Step 1: Start — every algorithm has its starting point.
  • Step 2: Define your algorithm's input, for example the rectangle's height and width to calculate its area.
  • Step 3: Define the variables, such as HEIGHT and WIDTH.
  • Step 4: Outline the operations, for example multiply HEIGHT and WIDTH and store the value in AREA.
  • Step 5: If, Else — use conditions to check some input data.
  • Step 6: Goto — transfer control to a certain step for some specific reason.
  • Step 7: Output the results of your operations.
  • Step 8: Stop — every algorithm must terminate after completing all steps.

Key Points

  • An algorithm is a sequence of steps to solve a problem.
  • Every algorithm starts with Start and ends with Stop.
  • A good algorithm is clear (definite) and finishes in finite steps.

lessons.title: Selection, Conditions and Loops
lessons.notes_html:
Selection is choosing between two actions when performing a task. In daily life we break activities into steps, and in each task we need to make a selection. For example, while doing homework, after completing one task we check whether we have answered all the questions: if a question remains unanswered, we attempt it, and we check again.

Conditions and IF Statements

A condition is a necessary requirement for action. We can write the condition in the form of a question, for example: Have All the Questions been Answered? The answer may be Yes or No: if Yes, we pack up our books; else we continue with the homework. Checking whether a condition is true or false is called testing the condition, and the condition is said to be True if the condition is met. The statement used to test a condition is if...then.

IF...THENIF...THEN...ELSE
Consists of two parts: in the first part the condition is tested, and if the condition is true, then execute the actions in the then part.Consists of three parts: the If part tells what the condition is; the Then part tells what to do if the condition is True; and the Else part tells what to do if the condition is false. Example: If there is still daylight, THEN ride a bicycle, ELSE clean your room.

Loops

A loop is a programming structure that repeats a sequence of instructions until a specific condition is True; in programming structure, we use a loop to repeat the statements. A finite loop executes its body a fixed number of times, while an infinite loop continues endlessly unless an external intervention occurs. Three common types are: the for loop, a count-controlled loop that iterates the number of times specified; the while loop, which iterates as long as the specified condition is true, and if the condition is false the code inside is never executed; and the do while loop, whose code block is executed at least once, even if the condition is false from the start.

Key Points

  • Selection means choosing between two actions.
  • Testing a condition checks whether it is true or false.
  • A loop repeats instructions until a condition is met.

lessons.title: Flowcharts and Their Symbols
lessons.notes_html:
A flowchart is a diagrammatic/graphical representation of a sequence of steps to solve a problem — a pictorial representation of the solution. The first design of flowchart was designed by John Von Neumann in 1945. A flowchart uses different standard symbols to design a solution, and each symbol is connected with arrows to show the flow of the processing; arrows are the symbol used for the flow of the program.

DiamondDecision making, where there are two or three alternatives, true and false. The diamond-shaped symbol is the decision symbol.
Arrows (flow lines)Indicate the flow of logic by connecting symbols
CircleConnector, used to replace long lines on a flowchart page
Off-page ConnectorUsed when the target is on another page
Subroutine SymbolA predefined process or function: a group of statements performing one processing task
PreparationPreprocessor or loops
CommentsAdded explanation within the specified range

Flowchart or Algorithm?

A flowchart is an excellent way of communicating the logic of a program, is easy and efficient for analyzing problems, acts as a blueprint that makes program development and maintenance easier, and is easy to convert into any programming language code. The basic requirements for creating a flowchart are input (taking data from the user), output (displaying the desired output), processing (the steps to solve the problem) and decision making (based on statements which are True or False). An algorithm is a written list of step-by-step instructions, usually faster to create; a flowchart takes more time because symbols must be drawn and arranged, but it is easier to understand at a glance.

Key Points

  • A flowchart is a pictorial representation of the solution of a problem.
  • The diamond is the decision symbol; the oval shows Start and End.
  • Arrows show the flow of the program.

lessons.title: Number Systems: Decimal, Binary and Hexadecimal
lessons.notes_html:
A computer is an electronic, digital device that stores, retrieves and processes data, usually in the binary number system, and can be programmed with instructions. It is composed of hardware and software. Charles Babbage is known as the Father of the Computer. Computers cannot understand words or numbers like humans, so everything is represented by a binary electrical signal of two states: ON (1) or OFF (0). Data in the form of digits is called digital data, and computers process and store data in binary form.

Number Systems

Anything which is used to count something is called a Number. There are 4 basic number systems: Decimal, Binary, Octal and Hexadecimal. In a positional notation system, the number base is called the radix.

SystemBase (radix)Digits used
Decimal100 to 9. The common system we use in daily life; also known as the Hindu-Arabic or Arabic number system. Each digit is multiplied by an appropriate power of 10 depending on its position, for example 654 = 6 x 100 + 5 x 10 + 4 x 1.
Binary20 and 1. Each position represents a specific power of the base 2. Computers, calculators and all digital devices use the binary system to store data and solve problems. There are 2 numbers in the binary system.
Hexadecimal160, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, A, B, C, D, E, F, where A = 10, B = 11, C = 12, D = 13, E = 14 and F = 15. It is the system that consists of both digits and letters, with 16 numbers in total.

Key Points

  • Computers store and process data in binary form: ON is 1, OFF is 0.
  • Decimal has base 10; binary has base 2; hexadecimal has base 16.
  • The base of a positional system is called its radix.

lessons.title: Converting Between Number Systems
lessons.notes_html:
We can convert any number system to another number system. Two methods are used for binary and decimal: the Multiplication method for binary to decimal, and the Division method for decimal to binary.

Binary to Decimal (Multiplication Method)

Each binary digit is multiplied by an appropriate power of 2, based on its position in the number. From the binary point to the left, start with power of 2 as 0, 1, 2, 3 and so on. Example: 110010 = 1 x 32 + 1 x 16 + 0 x 8 + 0 x 4 + 1 x 2 + 0 x 1 = 32 + 16 + 0 + 0 + 2 + 0 = 50. In the same way, 10101 = 21 and 1100100 = 100.

Decimal to Binary (Division Method)

  • Divide the number by 2 and keep track of the remainders.
  • Repeat the process with dividend equal to quotient till zero (0).
  • Read the remainders from bottom to top, from MSB (Most Significant Bit) to LSB (Least Significant Bit).

Example: 24 divided by 2 gives 12 remainder 0; 12 gives 6 remainder 0; 6 gives 3 remainder 0; 3 gives 1 remainder 1; 1 gives 0 remainder 1. Reading bottom to top: 24 = 11000 in binary. In the same way, 41 = 101001, 101 = 1100101, and 17 = 10001. For a fraction part, multiply the fraction by 2, keep track of the integer parts, and repeat until the fraction part is zero.

Hexadecimal Conversions

For hexadecimal to decimal, each hexadecimal digit is multiplied by an appropriate power of 16. Example: (ABC) in base 16 = 10 x 256 + 11 x 16 + 12 x 1 = 2560 + 176 + 12 = 2748. For decimal to hexadecimal, divide the number by 16 and keep track of the remainders. Hexadecimal and binary convert directly: separate the bits into groups of four and replace each group with the corresponding hexadecimal digit; and to go back, replace each hexadecimal digit with the corresponding 4-bit binary string.

Key Points

  • Binary to decimal uses the multiplication method.
  • Decimal to binary uses the division method; read remainders bottom to top.
  • One hexadecimal digit equals a group of 4 binary bits.

lessons.notes_html:
The capacity to store data in computer memory is measured in units built from the bit.

UnitMeaning
BitThe smallest unit of data in computing, which can be either 0 or 1. The term Bit is derived from Binary Digit. 0 means absence of electronic charge and 1 means presence of electric charge.
NibbleA group of 4 bits, which is half of a byte. For example, the binary number 1010 is a nibble.
ByteA group of 8 bits. One byte is a combination of 8 bits, and one character takes 1 byte in memory. A byte is the basic unit of measuring memory size.
WordA group of bytes that a computer processes at one time. Its size depends on the computer's architecture: often 2 bytes (16 bits), 4 bytes (32 bits) or 8 bytes (64 bits).

Larger Units

Each larger unit is 1024 times the one before: Kilobyte (KB) = 1024 bytes; Megabyte (MB) = 1024 x 1024 bytes; Gigabyte (GB) = (1024) cubed bytes; then Terabyte (TB), Petabyte (PB), Exabyte (EB), Zettabyte (ZB) and Yottabyte (YB).

Key Points

  • A bit is 0 or 1; a nibble is 4 bits; a byte is 8 bits.
  • 1 Kilobyte is 1024 bytes; 1 Gigabyte is (1024) cubed bytes.
  • A byte is the basic unit for measuring memory size.

lessons.title: Binary Addition and Subtraction
lessons.notes_html:
Binary arithmetic is performed column by column from the rightmost (least significant) bit, just like decimal arithmetic, but with only the digits 0 and 1.

Binary Addition Rules

AdditionResult
0 + 00
0 + 11
1 + 01
1 + 110 in binary: write 0 and carry 1 to the next column
1 + 1 + carried 111 in binary: write 1 and carry 1

Worked example: 1011 + 1110. Ones column: 1 + 0 = 1. Twos column: 1 + 1 = 10, write 0 carry 1. Fours column: 0 + 1 + carried 1 = 10, write 0 carry 1. Eights column: 1 + 1 + carried 1 = 11, write 1 carry 1. The final carry becomes a new leftmost bit, so the result is 11001. Check in decimal: 11 + 14 = 25, and 11001 is 25. In binary addition, 1 + 0 = 1.

Binary Subtraction Rules

SubtractionResult
0 - 00
1 - 01
1 - 10
0 - 1Cannot be done in that column: borrow 1 from the next higher column, which adds 2 to the present column, giving 2 - 1 = 1

Subtraction is also done column by column from the rightmost bit, with borrowing; when the next column is also 0, the borrow is carried further left until a 1 is found. Example from the unit: 1110001 - 11111 = 1010010. Check in decimal: 113 - 31 = 82, and 1010010 is 82.

Key Points

  • In binary, 1 + 1 = 10: write 0, carry 1.
  • Each carry is added into the next column to the left.
  • For 0 - 1, borrow 1 from the next column, which adds 2.

lessons.title: Data Representation and Coding Schemes
lessons.notes_html:
In a digital computer, any type of input or data (numbers, letters, special symbols, sound, picture or video) is first converted and transmitted as electrical pulses ON and OFF. Since computers work with binary digits only, all data must be converted into binary digits. Different schemes are used to convert data into binary digits; these schemes are called data encoding schemes. In ASCII and EBCDIC, the first four bits are called Zone bits and the remaining four bits represent the digit value.

SchemeBitsCharacters it can represent
ASCII — American Standard Code for Information Interchange. The most widely used coding scheme, developed by ANSI (American National Standards Institute).7-bit code128 characters, that is 2 to the power 7
EBCDIC — Extended Binary Coded Decimal Interchange Code. The standard character code for large computers.8-bit codeUp to 256 characters
BCD — Binary Coded Decimal. The simplest form of codes; each decimal digit is coded separately, for example 2 is 0010, and 234 uses 12 bits: 0010 0011 0100.4-bit codeOne decimal digit per 4 bits
Unicode — Universal Code. Widely used to convert mathematical and technical symbols using the UTF-8 coding scheme (Unicode Transformation Format-8). Unicode has started to replace ASCII codes.16-bit code65,536 characters

ASCII Example: Storing a Word

All characters on the keyboard are assigned a special code called ASCII. If we want to store ALI, the computer needs 3 bytes, one character taking 1 byte in memory: A's ASCII code is 65 and its binary code is 0100 0001; L's ASCII code is 76 and its binary code is 0100 1100; I's ASCII code is 73 and its binary code is 0100 1001. ASCII codes are of 7 bits, and the ASCII value of A is 65 and of a is 97, with each following letter taking the next value in order.

Key Points

  • ASCII is a 7-bit code for 128 characters.
  • EBCDIC is an 8-bit code; BCD is a 4-bit code; Unicode is a 16-bit code.
  • Every keyboard character has its own ASCII code.

lessons.notes_html:
Scratch Programming deals with creating a script with the help of blocks. The interface has these basic components:

  • Menu bar — the top bar that typically contains options like File, Edit and View.
  • Green flag and red stop sign — common controls used to start and stop code execution. The Stop button is used to stop the project at the time of execution.
  • Tabs — the navigation tabs or sections: Scripts (labelled Code in the newer interface), Costumes and Sounds.
  • Project name — the name assigned to the current project.
  • Scripts Area — the main coding area where the program logic is developed.
  • Stage — the main working area in Scratch: the area where the animated characters or objects are displayed and their behaviours are implemented.
  • Blocks Area — the section that contains the various programming blocks or commands used to build the program.
  • Sprite List — the list of animated characters or objects that are part of the project.

Sprites

In Scratch, the objects are known as Sprites. A sprite is an object or character which you see on stage. The default sprite in Scratch is the Scratch Cat. Each sprite has its own scripting area. To add a new sprite: in the new sprite panel, choose a sprite from the library, or choose Upload sprite from file and change its name by clicking on the sprite; go to the Costumes tab and use the shrink option above the painting board to reduce its size if needed; and drag the sprite on the stage to place it where you want it. lessons.title: Blocks, Scripts and Moving a Sprite
lessons.notes_html:
Blocks are the programming commands in the Blocks Area. The block categories are Motion, Looks, Sound, Events, Control, Sensing, Operators, Variables and My Blocks. Blocks are dragged into the Scripts Area and snapped together. A script is the collection of stepwise instructions given to a sprite, built by snapping blocks together. A Hat Block is used to start a script, for example when green flag clicked. The CAP block is used to end the script, and Repeat is a block to replay an action for a specific number of times.

Motion Blocks

  • Motion block controls the movements of the sprite; the move block moves the sprite by a specified number of steps.
  • Direction block is used to rotate the sprite at a given angle, and the circular Arrow enables full rotation of the sprite.
  • Point Towards block changes the direction of the sprite; Go to x: y: places the sprite at a given value of the x and y axes; the glide block moves it smoothly to a position.
  • Boolean block is used to hold logical values such as True or False, and the touching block is in the Sensing category: Sensing blocks let a sprite detect what is around it, such as touching another sprite, the mouse-pointer or an edge.
  • The Pen Clear block removes all marks made by pens and stamps.

Two Move Programs

To move a sprite yourself: open a new project, open the Code section and select Motion, drag the move steps block into the Scripts Area; the default Scratch Cat is created, and when you press on the block, the cat moves ten steps. To move a sprite automatically: place blocks that set the x-axis as -240 and y-axis as 0, set the size to 25 percent of the sprite, add a glide block with x as 150, y as 0 and glide 5 seconds, and press the Green Flag to execute the program — the sprite moves without any intervention for 5 seconds.

Key Points

  • Click on the Scripts (Code) tab to write a script.
  • A Hat Block starts a script; a CAP block ends it.
  • Motion blocks control the movements of the sprite.

lessons.title: Working with Many Sprites: Broadcast Messages
lessons.notes_html:
A Scratch project can have many sprites, and each sprite has its own scripting area. When you want one sprite to do a certain action only when another sprite commands it, you use the broadcast protocol: one sprite broadcasts a message and the other sprite starts a script only when the message is received.

The Two Broadcast Blocks

BlockWhat it does
Broadcast MessageAn Event block and a stack block which sends a broadcast throughout the whole Scratch program, without any waits in its script.
When I ReceiveAn Event block and a Hat block. Scripts that begin with this block will be invoked once the specified broadcast has been sent by a calling script.

The Cat and Bat Project

In the unit's project there are two sprites, a cat and a flying bat, on a Brick Wall 1 background. The bat's flying script starts when the green flag is pressed: it glides to the coordinate (-150, 80), then forever switches costume between bat1-a and bat1-b with a wait of 0.5 seconds, which makes the flying animation. When you press Space, the cat's script runs: it says Fly Bat for 2 seconds and broadcasts Fly Bat. The bat's receiving script then says Ok Cat for 1 second and glides in 2 seconds to a random position on the X axis, using the Pick random block to get a random number between -150 and 150, at y: 80. Start the project with the green flag.

Key Points

  • Every sprite has its own scripting area.
  • Broadcast sends a message to the whole program.
  • When I Receive starts a script when that message arrives.

lessons.title: Variables and the Countdown Timer
lessons.notes_html:
A variable is a named value that a program can store and change while it runs. Variables can increase a value, for example increase the score when the player touches a sprite, or decrease a value, for example a countdown timer. Timers make any game more interesting: their main function is to add stakes to the game, because if the player runs out of time while playing, they lose.

Creating a Variable

  • Navigate to the Variables section of the block menu.
  • Click the Make a Variable button, which takes you to a new screen to create your new variable.
  • Enter a new variable name; make it descriptive, for example Time Remaining, and make sure the For all sprites option is selected, so all sprites in your project can access the variable.
  • Click OK.
  • Check the box to the left of the variable in the block menu; this tells Scratch to display the variable on the stage, making it visible to the player.

How the Countdown Timer Works

  • The timer begins running when the green flag is clicked: set Time Remaining to 60.
  • The timer runs in a loop: repeat 60 times — wait 1 second, then change Time Remaining by -1.
  • After repeating 60 times, Time Remaining is equal to 0 and the loop is finished.
  • The script then says Game Over! for 2 seconds, and the stop all block brings the rest of the game to a halt.

Sounds are added in the same style: select the sprite, open its Sounds tab to add a sound from the sound library, then use the play sound block from the Sound category in your script. In the unit's Guessing Game project, two variables are used together: one holds the random number the host is thinking about (Host Number, which you hide), and the other is the answer variable supplied by Scratch for the user's guess, inside a loop that answers too high or too low.

Key Points

  • A variable stores a value that can change while the program runs.
  • Create variables from the Variables section with Make a Variable.
  • A countdown timer sets a variable and decreases it by 1 every second.

lessons.title: Digital Citizenship and ICT Ethics
lessons.notes_html:
Digital citizenship is the responsible practice of the knowledge and technology skills by the technology consumers, and the responsible use of the internet and digital devices to participate with the society. It is also defined as the norms of appropriate and responsible behavior regarding technology use. The Internet itself is a network of networks: the largest network in the world, in which all computers and devices are connected with each other, and internet access is established by ISPs (Internet Service Providers) through Wi-Fi signals, mobile phones, public internet, hotspots, broadband and cable.

Digital Ethics and ICT Ethics

Ethics is a set of moral principles that govern the behavior of an individual or group of people. Digital ethics, also known as information ethics, are the standards that ensure respect for users on the internet — the norms dedicated to ensuring the respect of others. ICT Ethics deals with the procedure, values and practice that govern the process of using ICT and its related disciplines without damaging the moral values of an individual or organization. Examples include intellectual property rights, privacy policies and online etiquette. The aims of ICT Ethics are: ensuring access to right information; ensuring information integrity and security; enforcing online etiquette; enforcing the right to privacy; and enforcing the copyrights of information.

Guidelines for Ethical Use of ICT Devices

  • Do not use a computer to harm other people.
  • Do not interfere with other people's computer work.
  • Do not use or copy software for which you have not paid.
  • Do not use other people's computer resources without authorization.
  • Do not appropriate other people's intellectual property.

The three key areas to be aware of are Copyright, Plagiarism and Digital Piracy, covered in the next lesson.

Key Points

  • A digital citizen uses the internet and devices responsibly.
  • Digital ethics is also known as information ethics.
  • Never use a computer to harm others or copy unpaid software.

lessons.title: Copyright, Plagiarism and Piracy
lessons.notes_html:
Three important words protect the work of creators. Learn the difference between them.

TermMeaning
CopyrightA form of legal protection that gives ownership rights to your original works. It protects the rights of an author for their original work: no one can copy your work, even published or unpublished, and it protects the author from unauthorized duplication, distribution or other use. In other words, copyright is a right to copy, if the author of the work allows you to copy or reproduce the work.
PlagiarismUsing someone else's words or ideas without properly crediting the original author: using someone else's words as yours. For example, copying text and pasting it into a new document, and submitting a full document that is not your own.
PiracyDigital piracy refers to the illegal copying or distribution of copyrighted material via the Internet, when someone replicates a copy of a work of others and sells it without permission. It negatively affects the creative industries, including software, film, publishing, music and gaming.

Copyright Exclusive Rights

  • The right to control duplication of the work.
  • The right to control the spreading and sale of the work.
  • The right to control the display of the work or perform publicly.
  • It helps to generate derivative works based on the original work.

The ethics rules are: no one should use anyone's creative work — a song, a video, a movie clip, a piece of visual art, a photograph — without authorization or compensation of the owner; no one should use someone else's work without giving proper credit to the original owner or creator; and no one should replicate another's creative work, software, songs, videos or books.

Key Points

  • Copyright is legal protection that gives ownership rights.
  • Plagiarism is using someone else's words as your own.
  • Piracy is replicating and selling copies of others' work without permission.

lessons.title: Privacy, Confidentiality and Securing Your Information
lessons.notes_html:
Online privacy, also known as internet privacy, refers to how much of your personal, financial and browsing data remains private when you are online. Confidentiality of information involves restricting data access strictly to authorized personnel, and users have a responsibility to maintain secure access control systems, for example passwords. An ATM card number is an example of confidentiality.

Steps to Secure Information Privacy and Confidentiality

  • Never give out your name, address, phone number, e-mail, password or school name to unrelated people or strangers.
  • Never share a picture of yourself with strangers.
  • Never open e-mails, files or web pages from unknown sources or persons.
  • Always check with your teacher or parent before downloading any information or application.
  • Never respond to strangers online, and tell your teacher or parents if something makes you uncomfortable, scared or confused, or if anyone online asks you to meet in person.
  • Never share your movement plans or location on social networks, and never enter an online chat room without an adult's presence.
  • Do not share details about your life with others online, avoid abusive language while chatting on social media, and do not buy or order anything online without parents' supervision.
  • Don't save personal information on public devices.

Email Care

Do not create, forward or share spam, and use a spam filter; do not send or attach confidential documents and sensitive data in emails; do not open unexpected attachments and links in emails containing unwanted material; do not access, copy or transmit another's messages without permission; and do not share electronic communications that contain religious or political beliefs and abusive language. You should not open emails and attachments from a suspicious source, and it is necessary to regularly change our password.

Key Points

  • Never share personal details, pictures or location with strangers online.
  • Confidentiality means only authorized people can access the data.
  • Check with a teacher or parent before downloading anything.

lessons.title: Phishing, Social Engineering and Staying Protected
lessons.notes_html:
Phishing is the most popular digital social engineering attack, and a cybercrime in which personal information is obtained by email or phones. It is a trick used to steal money, identity, and personal information like credit card numbers, bank information or passwords. The phishers are individuals or illegal groups who pretend to be from reputable organizations, friends and family. They communicate through email, telephone or text message and use a true appearance, with fake e-mails to collect information from users, or connect them to a fake website.

Social Engineering and Social Hacking

Social engineering is an approach of using and cheating a victim or target to gain control of a computer system, to take someone's personal and financial information; it focuses on psychological tactics to exploit human behavior. Example: an attacker sends an email pretending to be from a company's IT department, asking the victim to reset their password using a fake link. Social hacking is a subset of social engineering that specifically refers to using social interactions to gain unauthorized access to systems or data, often by blending into a social environment to gather information or gain trust. Example: an attacker pretends to be a delivery person to gain access to a secure building. Social hacking is also known as social engineering.

Staying Protected

  • Antivirus must be installed in the computer to save it from virus, and kept updated.
  • Use strong and complex passwords and change and update them regularly.
  • Use Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) to add an additional layer of security to your accounts.
  • Avoid clicking on suspicious links or downloading attachments from unknown sources, and be wary of tempting offers: if an offer sounds too enticing, think twice before accepting it as a fact.

Key Points

  • Phishing steals personal information through fake emails, calls or messages.
  • Social engineering cheats people to gain access to systems and data.
  • Antivirus, strong passwords and 2FA protect your accounts.

lessons.title: Cyberbullying and Media Bias
lessons.notes_html:
Cyberbullying is the use of digital platforms and technology to harass, intimidate or harm others. It includes sending, posting or sharing negative, harmful or mean content about someone else, and it can occur through various online channels.

Where Cyberbullying Happens

  • Social Media — platforms like Facebook, Instagram, Twitter and TikTok: posting hurtful comments, spreading rumors, or sharing embarrassing photos.
  • Messaging Apps — platforms like WhatsApp, Snapchat, Messenger and Telegram: sending threatening or abusive messages, or creating group chats to exclude or target someone.
  • Online Games — multiplayer games like Fortnite, Minecraft or Call of Duty: harassing other players, sending mean messages, or using voice chat to insult or threaten others.
  • Email — platforms like Gmail, Yahoo Mail and Outlook: sending bullying emails, threatening messages, or bombarding someone with unwanted emails.
  • Forums and Websites — platforms like Reddit, online discussion boards and comment sections: posting negative comments, spreading false information, or attacking individuals in discussions.

Media Bias

A bias is when media takes one side of the parties. A good digital citizen evaluates digital media bias and messaging instead of believing everything at once, and stands up for and supports the victim of cyberbullying rather than joining the bully or standing by silently.

Key Points

  • Cyberbullying is harassing or harming others through digital platforms.
  • It happens on social media, messaging apps, games, email and forums.
  • Bias means the media takes one side of the parties.

lessons.title: Threats to Devices and Data, and the Impact of Social Media
lessons.notes_html:
The internet brings threats to your devices and data. The unit's main threats and protections are:

  • Deletion of Data Accidentally — a good user can delete his own data accidentally. Solutions: proper rights must be given to the user by the administrator, and periodic backups of data should be taken to recover deleted files.
  • Firewalls — computers are not always secure, so we must use firewalls to protect data from unauthorized access. A firewall is a security system designed to monitor and control incoming and outgoing network traffic based on predetermined security rules; it acts as a barrier between a trusted internal network and untrusted external networks, such as the internet.
  • Virus — a type of malicious software designed to infect and damage computer systems by spreading from one file to another, often without the user's knowledge. A computer virus, when executed, replicates itself and inserts its own code into other files and programs. Protection: install and regularly update antivirus software, avoid downloading files or clicking links from unknown sources, keep your operating system and applications updated, and back up important data.
  • Natural Hazards — hardware (data storage) can be damaged by fire, floods, earthquake or falling of buildings, so save backups away from the computer room.
  • Hackers — hacking is the unauthorized access to or manipulation of computer systems, networks or data. Protection: strong passwords changed regularly, Two-Factor Authentication (2FA), regular updates, avoiding suspicious links and attachments, and avoiding public Wi-Fi for sensitive transactions (use a VPN if necessary).

Social Media: Positive and Negative Impact

lessons.title: Entrepreneurship and Digital Entrepreneurship
lessons.notes_html:
Entrepreneurship is an ability to establish and run a business enterprise: a fresh starting of a business with some doubts about profit, but the aim is making profit, finding opportunities, and taking risks to establish and grow a new business. An entrepreneur is an individual who creates a new business, bearing most of the risks and enjoying most of the rewards, commonly seen as an innovator, a source of new ideas, goods, services, and business or procedures.

Characteristics of Entrepreneurship

  • Identifying Opportunities — identifying needs or problems that people have, which can be solved with new products or services.
  • Innovative Solutions — creating new and unique ideas, products or services that stand out.
  • Risk-Taking — investing time, money and resources into a venture with the potential for both high rewards and high risks.
  • Resource Management — efficiently managing resources, including finances, personnel and technology.
  • Business Growth — scaling the business to increase market reach, revenue and impact.

Digital Entrepreneurship

Digital entrepreneurship is the smart application of the power of digital technologies to business: the process of using digital technologies to start, manage and run businesses, using the internet, mobile devices, social media and other digital tools to create, deliver and scale products or services. It includes identifying opportunities to reach and find customers; designing and presenting new products and services; generating income and reducing the cost of products and services; and cooperating with partners to manage risk and competitive advantage. Its three principal components are the vision, the technology and the strategy. It is not just a computer business: it can apply to different sectors of the economy, for example agriculture, trading, manufacturing, education and real estate, and to both an existing business and a new business.

Key Points

  • Entrepreneurship means establishing and running a new business.
  • Digital entrepreneurship applies digital technologies to business.
  • Vision, technology and strategy are its three components.

lessons.title: Design Thinking and Its Five Steps
lessons.notes_html:
Design thinking is a non-linear, iterative process that teams use to understand users, challenge assumptions, redefine problems and create innovative solutions to prototype and test. It is a human-centered approach: it creates the space for the end-users and identifies the needs and demands of the target audience, and it encourages a mind to move from just problem solving to identifying the opportunities for significant impact. Traditional problem solving involves coming up with one solution, but design thinking first makes us diverge, by trying to generate a diverse assortment of possible alternative solutions to a problem. Design thinking involves five phases: Empathize, Define, Ideate, Prototype and Test.

The Five Steps

  • Empathize — research your users' needs. Gain real insight into users and their needs through user-centric research: consult specialists, make observations, and immerse yourself in your users' physical environment. Empathy allows design thinkers to set aside their own assumptions and gain real insight into users and their needs.
  • Define — state your users' needs and problems. Organize the information gathered during the Empathize stage, analyze your observations, and define the core problems and the problem statement in a human-centered manner.
  • Ideate — challenge assumptions and create ideas. With a solid background from the first two stages, look at the problem from different perspectives and ideate innovative solutions to your problem statement.
  • Prototype — start to create solutions. Produce a number of inexpensive, scaled-down versions of the product, or specific features within it, to investigate the key solutions generated in the ideation phase. A prototype is a simple sample of your future design, or a test case that demonstrates the finished product.

lessons.title: Design Thinking Examples and Sustainable Development
lessons.notes_html:
The unit gives five real-world examples of design thinking in entrepreneurship. Airbnb (Air bed and Breakfast) identified the pain points of travelers, tourists and explorers, and provided unique, affordable accommodations, building a trust environment between hosts and guests. Dropbox, a cloud-based file storage service, recognized the frustration users faced with traditional file storage and sharing, and developed a simple and natural solution to store, access, synchronize and share files from anywhere safely. Tesla addresses the rising demand for sustainable transportation with high-performance electric vehicles like the Model S, Model 3, Model X and Model Y. Netflix is the unit's detailed example: in 2011 it responded to consumers' need for original, provoking content that was not airing on old networks, and in 2016 it added short trailers to the interface — Netflix is an example of design thinking. Nike focuses on creating new and groundbreaking products for its consumers, and has been a favorite brand among athletes for nearly five decades.

Sustainable Development

Sustainable development is development that meets the needs of the present, without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. It balances different, and often competing, needs against an awareness of the environmental, social and economic limitations we face as a society. Its five pillars are: People (end poverty and hunger in all forms and ensure dignity and equality), Planet (protect our planet's natural resources and climate for future generations), Prosperity (ensure prosperous and fulfilling lives in harmony with nature), Partnership (implement the agenda through a solid global partnership) and Peace (foster peaceful, just and inclusive societies). The three types of sustainable development are economic viability, environmental protection and social equity. The unit's examples are wind energy, solar energy, green environment, sustainable construction and sustainable forestry.

Achieving the Goals

Sustainable development can be achieved by limiting human activities; technological development should be input effective and not input utilizing; the rate of consumption should not surpass the rate of recovery; all types of pollution should be minimized; and by sensible use of natural resources — promoting the kind of development that minimizes environmental problems, for example quality education and zero hunger.

Key Points

  • Netflix, Airbnb, Dropbox, Tesla and Nike are design thinking examples.
  • Sustainable development meets present needs without harming future generations.
  • Its examples include wind energy, solar energy and sustainable forestry.
